1.1: 1.1 Argument. After the Corinthians had done penance, the Apostle writes them a consolatory Epistle from Troas by Titus; and praising them he exhorts them to better things, showing that they had been saddened indeed but amended. Paul an apostle. First, in his usual way, he sets the greeting. Then he gives thanks to God for the goods conferred by grace, speaking to the perfect: afterwards by his own example he invites to endurance of suffering; next he refutes the false apostles by putting them down, uncovering their cunning. And he commends himself in many ways. At last a moral admonition is added with a repeated blessing. Setting the greeting first, against false pride he names himself Paul; and against presumption of heart, apostle, saying: Paul, etc.
1.2: 1.2 Blessed. First he speaks to the perfect about tribulation, setting himself forth as an example of patience and of consolation received from God, counting as praise what to others is disgrace. God. Creator of all. Father of the Lord. Through whom he is also ours. Father of mercies. A father giving pardon of sins, and good works, and constancy in tribulation. And God. Giver of all perfect consolation: as much as it is fitting for God to give to those who suffer for Christ. That God is of consolation is clear from this, that he consoles.
1.4: 1.4 With which we exhort. That is, which God gave for this, not only to console, but also to exhort: and so our consolation avails also to exhort others, that we may truly be able to console.
1.9: 1.9 We ourselves. Not only others about us, but also in us, etc., because our nature promised nothing but death or failure. He signifies that so great an insolence of the wicked had risen against the preachers of the faith that they had death before their eyes. For they were so afflicted that they despaired of the present life. But because God does not refuse his helps to those placed in despair, especially to his own, he rescued them despairing of themselves but trusting in God. For they professed that under excessive pressure they would have failed unless God had been present.
1.10: 1.10 And he delivered. God does not refuse his helps to his own placed in necessity.
1.12: 1.12 For our glory. Therefore both you and others ought to pray for us. Or therefore your prayers will be able to help us: because that in which we glory is so honorable, namely: The testimony. They are good works, which testify outwardly what is in the conscience. The testimony, that is a conscience not reproaching but witnessing that in simplicity, etc. In the sincerity of God. As conscience is a great punishment to the wicked, so is it joy to the pious. Not as though proudly glorying in it, but giving all to God; therefore he rightly does not say: Our glory is the testimony of another's malice or of lesser grace, but of our conscience. Which, because it is hidden, is not subject to another's judgment, and therefore let no one presume to think or pronounce a sentence against it. Not in carnal wisdom. It belongs to carnal wisdom to love pleasures, avoid labors, or to preach according to the natures of things and not against them, as the false apostles did, whose painted preaching he rebukes.
1.13: 1.13 But I hope. He hopes they are advancing, because they had begun to become better, having learned the Apostle's affection toward them, and they gloried in him.
1.14: 1.14 That we are your glory. You will know that you ought to obtain glory, that is eternal glory, through us, and we through you well instructed, which would not be so if we received offenses from you.
1.15: 1.15 In this confidence. Because the life of some was clean or amended, he wished to see those whom before it was unworthy to see. If therefore he did not go, he wished it understood that there were some among them on account of whom the Apostle did not fulfill his will, who ought to take pains to purify themselves now. I wished to come to you first, that you might have a second grace, etc. First, because in the former Epistle he had promised that he would come, and had not come: and therefore he seemed false and light, which he now excuses. For he did not do this except for their fault. He is not to be judged a liar who says what is false which he thinks true: because as far as he is concerned he does not deceive, but is deceived. On the other hand he lies who says what is true which he thinks false, nor is he free from lying; he who with his mouth unknowingly speaks the truth, but knowing it not to be true, lies by will.
1.17: 1.17 That with me there should be Yes and No. That is, that I should put will before usefulness; as if he said: Not so, because usefulness is to be put before will, and so I did.
1.18: 1.18 But God is faithful, for our word which was with you is not, etc. As if he said: In this I am not to be believed a liar, because in nothing else have I lied to you. And this can be believed, because God is faithful, who promised teachers of the truth.
1.20: 1.20 To our glory. Because by this we are proved to preach true things. I say ours, for I do not attribute so much to us, but to God, because it is God who confirms.
1.21: 1.21 With you in Christ. Then if you are firm in Christ, it is the more evident concerning us, through whom you have been confirmed.
1.23: 1.23 But I, etc. As if he said: I did not give it up for lightness or earthly advantage, but sparing you. The spiritual man does not carry out what he has arranged when he meditates something more providently for salvation. Not that we lord it. Lest they be indignant as at lordship, because he had said, sparing you I did not come, he adds: Not that we lord it, etc.
2.1: 2.1 But I determined. Sparing you I did not come, but I determined this same thing: which I promised when I sent the first epistle, namely not to come again; or that there should not again be sadness as there was, having heard of their sins.
2.2: 2.2 For if I make you sad. By correcting, rebuking in any way, whether by letter or presence.
2.4: 2.4 Not that you should be made sad. For the Apostle rebuked for this, to show with what love he loved them, grieving more than they over their sins; he who does not rebuke with this affection saddens. For he insults who does not sympathize with his brother.
2.5: 2.5 But if any has caused sadness. He commands that fornicator, whom he had earlier indicated was to be delivered to Satan, to be received, because he had been corrected. But in part, not to burden, etc. I do not lay the burden of sadness on all, for the sake of those who have grieved over their sins.
2.6: 2.6 This rebuke, which is made by many so that on the contrary more. Which, even if by the length of time or by some other measure it seems a penalty not sufficiently worthy, yet in this is not to be reckoned small, that it is done by many, by whom, gathered together, he was delivered to Satan. He certainly suffers great grief who sees many abhor his crime. And so it suffices that he be rebuked by many.
2.7: 2.7 Forgive and console. Rightly he commands to forgive a man afflicted for his sin and to help him through consolations. For if, corrected, he grieves in soul, he soon has fruit. For this is true penance, to cease from sin.
2.9: 2.9 For to this end also I wrote. Since I wrote for the sake of receiving him, I also wrote for this, that I might know whether those whom I have found obedient to me in the casting out will be obedient in all things in the future.
2.11: 2.11 That we be not circumvented. Therefore we ought to pardon, lest we be deceived by Satan through excessive harshness. For often, because of harsher punishments, the weak is precipitated into despair.
2.12: 2.12 When I came to Troas, etc. After the interposition about receiving the fornicator, he returns to them, showing that as it was their fault that he did not come to Corinth, so that he did not succeed at Troas, while Titus was detained among them, without whom he could not succeed there, because perhaps Titus could use their language more expressly.
2.13: 2.13 Because I did not. Because alone he could not instruct the faithful, and at the same time resist the clamoring unbelievers.
2.14: 2.14 The odor of knowledge, etc. That is Christ, who like an odor proceeding from the Father makes him known though invisible: as some thing which is not seen is known by its smell, and in what place it is is understood. Or understand by the name of odor the miracles or the words of doctrine by which one comes to knowledge of him.
2.15: 2.15 A good odor. Namely, as formerly the legal victim, so now the true preaching and sincere reputation of the apostles. The odor of God the Father is Christ: the odor of Christ are the apostles, in whose life and preaching Christ is shown, not blasphemed. As it is said of the wicked: The name of the Lord is blasphemed through you among the Gentiles.
2.16: 2.16 An odor of death. So that from our preaching death proceeds, to those rushing thence into eternal damnation.
2.17: 2.17 As many. Here he touches the false apostles, who by corrupt doctrine violated the truth, of whom Isaiah says: Your vintners mix water with the wine.
3.1: 3.1 Do we begin again. Because he knew they took his commendation amiss, as in the first Epistle, as if he sought his own glory; he begins to show against their opinion that he seeks not his own glory but God's.
3.3: 3.3 Written not. You are a representation of Christ and of me, and this is firmly written in our hearts, not erasably like what is written with ink: or not with the foul marks of heretical perversity, of those who interweave heresies. Not on tables. Stone signifies nothing but a most hardened will, and inflexible against God. Fleshly. That is, having feeling, not stony without feeling.
3.4: 3.4 Confidence. He said he did not need letters, now he says that he does not commend himself but Christ; as if he said: You are the epistle of Christ, and ours, but the confidence of saying such things we refer not to you but to God.
3.5: 3.5 Not that we are sufficient. AUGUSTINE, book 2, against two letters of the Pelagians, ch. 8. Who does not see that to think comes before to believe? For no one believes anything unless he has first thought it ought to be believed. Although even to believe is nothing else than to think with assent. If therefore to think good is not from us, neither is to believe. But our sufficiency. Let those attend here and weigh these words who think that the beginning of faith is from us, and its completion from God. For he commends grace, which is not given according to any merits, but produces all good merits.
3.6: 3.6 Who also has made us fit. Here he commends himself by the dignity of the office, namely of the Gospel, preferring himself not only to the false apostles who preach carnal observances, but even to Moses himself, minister of the law.
3.9: 3.9 Much more abounds. That is, in praise than the old: because the glory of God is more in salvation than in death. For although he justly condemns what was done under the law, yet it contributes more to his praise if he forgives, that the guilty may be able to correct himself; which is afforded by grace in the New Testament.
3.10: 3.10 For neither. It truly abounds, so that in comparison with it that is not to be called glory. That which was glorious. Namely Moses in this aforesaid part, that is in the face. Or it is not glorious in this part, that is with respect to this part of ours. For that was as great as was fitting to be believed of a servant. This, however, is as great as is that of the Son of the Father: for Christ is in the glory of God the Father, so that there is as great a difference between the glory of Moses and of Christ as between the image and the truth.
3.12: 3.12 Having. That is, the dignity of the New and Old Testament having been shown, he shows the use of each. Much confidence. By use we exercise ourselves in good works whence confidence grows in us. For we shall see as much as we believe, and because the glory is open, we do not conceal our meaning, as Moses did, but speak openly.
3.14: 3.14 The same. Because they do not understand otherwise now than before the coming of Christ. Which is done away in Christ. Hence at the passion of Christ the veil of the temple was torn, to signify that by the passion of Christ the sacraments of the law and prophecy are revealed. He says veil in comparison with prophecy, that it might not be understood.
3.15: 3.15 But until, etc. For those who are in Christ it is done away: but upon their heart is a veil, that is blindness weighing down their reason: when, that is although, Moses is read, that is expounded, to them. And so two things hinder, why they do not understand: both the veil, that is obscurity, is in the reading, and blindness upon the hearts, and this until this present day.
3.16: 3.16 But when he shall be converted. That is when their mind, having laid aside hardness of heart and its own blindness, shall be converted by believing. The veil shall be taken away. As in water wine is understood to be hidden, for all prophecy, Christ not being understood, is something insipid and foolish.
3.17: 3.17 Now the Lord is the Spirit. The order of the words is: The Holy Spirit is the Lord, that is he can do what he wills, and therefore enlightens whom he wills; and leaves in darkness whom he wills. Wherever the spirit of the Lord is, that is of the Son, through whom the Holy Spirit is given, there is liberty: and therefore the Jews, who do not have the spirit, cannot understand freely as we. Or, the Lord to whom they are converted is spirit, that is spiritual essence, and so causes them to understand spiritually.
3.18: 3.18 But we all with face unveiled. In which for the Jews there is a veil. In a mirror nothing but an image is seen. We therefore strive that through this image, that is reason, that we are, we may see in some measure him by whom we were made, as through a mirror. Into the same image. Because the same image of God is the glory of God, as above: The man indeed is the image and glory of God.
4.2: 4.2 Commending. That your light may shine before men. Before God. Not that they may be seen by men.
4.4: 4.4 In whom. The order of the words can be this: In whom perishing the true and just God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age. The god of this age. That is the God who not only rules the good but also casts down the wicked according to merit, giving them what they want, that is that they not believe: which malice does not do, but justice. Or, god of the age, pride or gluttony, or the devil prince of the world, who rules over the worldly.
4.5: 4.5 For not. As if he said: I rightly say of the glory of Christ, or: We have commended ourselves before God in the manifestation of truth, and we do other such things; and this for Christ's sake.
4.6: 4.6 Light to shine. Which was in the separation of the elements. For darkness began, from the time the confused mass of heaven and earth began to be: afterwards light coming, what was made is rendered better. In which the affection of a man advancing is signified, hence: You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord, Ephesians 5. In the face of Jesus. This is the sense: Since the divine nature does not fall under the sight, through the assumed humanity shining with divine light and sending forth lightnings it is beheld, so that it may be. Hence it is also manifest that God did not send in unbelief, who furnished abundantly to all the splendor of the understanding light: but they themselves loved unbelief, and he did not furnish the ray to them when they would not look. Of the brightness of knowledge. The knowledge of the glory of God is that by which we know that there is a light by which our darkness is lit.
4.7: 4.7 We have. So far he has dealt with the height of knowledge: here with the frailty of the flesh, which is toward glory, though it seems the contrary. Treasure. The sacrament of God, which is dispensed to the faithful, is hidden from the faithless; he affirms it is a treasure.
4.10: 4.10 Always the dying, etc. There is no doubt that in the martyrs Christ is slain, and in those who suffer for the faith, either death, or chains, or scourges are the passions of Christ, that his life also may be made manifest in their body. For passions are what show merit for the future life, which Christ promised, hence in another place he says: When I am weak, then I am strong, and again: Through many tribulations, etc. Be made manifest. For some doubted about the resurrection.
4.12: 4.12 So then death, etc. Because through death we obtain the life of Jesus: therefore death is not useless, but works something great in us. But the life in which you delight in earthly things works in you eternal death. Or passively: therefore, that is on account of the hope of the life of Jesus, death works, that is is effected in us by the aforesaid passions, that is we permit it to be effected: but through this life is effected in you, that is faith is planted.
4.14: 4.14 With you. Not you with us, as inferiors, but that you may be equal to us, if you will. And I assert well of you that we do all these things for the sake of instructing you by our example. So all things concern you: that the grace of God abounding in us may abound in you, and through you in others, and through you may abound in many with thanksgiving, that you and they may give thanks to God. To the glory of God, that is to show God glorious.
5.1: 5.1 For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, which a building, etc. That is we shall have an immortal body, if the body be dissolved through tribulations, and therefore, since it will so be dissolved, that the condition and cause may be premised. Not made with hands, but eternal. That is not made by the complexion of men, namely, not produced by the aid of human generation nor increased by human nourishment, but ineffably fashioned by God. Eternal. Because in it there will be remaining without end.
5.2: 5.2 For. Not only for the present dwelling, but also, in this, that is in the consideration of this so great glory, we groan. From the delay of desire: which we would not do unless we were certain. In figure of this matter Achsah, daughter of Caleb, asked for the upper watering and the lower watering, that we may pour forth tears not only for the misery of the present sojourn, but for the delay of heavenly glory. We groan, because we desire over and above the invocation of the soul, which we have already received. From heaven. That is, we wish to have an immortal and impassible body, in the likeness of the heavenly ones. For even he who, etc. As if he said: We, more perfect, groan for the delay, because even the less perfect, who cherish the flesh. Among these the Apostle numbers himself, lest they think less of themselves.
5.3: 5.3 If yet being clothed with the glory of the promise; not naked. The saints desire this, lest, rising again with the body received, they be found naked, that is strangers to the promised glory. For this is the work: that clothed with the body they may be clothed over with glory, which is the change in brightness. Burdened with that body: by which yet we do not wish death to be taken from us, but to be clothed over, that is clothed by God with the robe of immortality which destroys mortality, not that it come upon it.
5.4: 5.4 We who are in the tabernacle. Who love the dwelling of this body, about which care is not to be taken, since it is only a tabernacle for a time, we groan with desire of the heavenly. I say we burdened, as if he said: No wonder if we groan: because we are far from blessedness. For even of this lesser thing we groan, because we are stripped of this body. By it. That is, therefore we groan. Because we do not wish to be stripped, if this could be done. Or, we groan, with desire of the heavenly. But God has effected this. Or, we do not wish to be stripped: yet God has caused us to desire immortality. That may be swallowed up, etc. So that mortality be nowhere. Not below, not above, not within, not without. For death is swallowed up in victory.
5.6: 5.6 Being bold. God makes us wish for immortality, and makes us certain by the Spirit, and therefore we are bold. We are absent from the Lord. How? since elsewhere it is written: In him we live and move and are, Acts 17? Because although God is everywhere, he is not seen here as in heaven. We are absent therefore not by faith, but by sight.
5.10: 5.10 That every one may receive. Even children, who, if not by themselves, by others have done things, since through them they believed or did not believe, are judged according to this, not according to what they would have done had they lived long. For he says: according to what he has done in the body, not as he would have done if he had lived; in vain therefore does a man promise himself after this body what he neglected to prepare here in the body. We persuade. The apostles persuade that the rest, living well, may believe and provide for themselves, because by the perverse speech of some the day of the Lord is brought into doubt.
5.11: 5.11 But to God we are made manifest, because we preach what God commands.
5.13: 5.13 For whether in mind. As if he said: Of us certainly you can glory, because whatever we do is either the honor of God or the profit of our neighbor. Whether we are beside ourselves, that is, if we commend ourselves (in which we are thought senseless), it is to God, that is to the honor of God, who thus exalted us. Whether sober: that we may not speak high things of ourselves, it is for your profit. For whether we are beside ourselves in mind. The Apostle speaks of a certain ineffable contemplation and rapture, where he heard what it is not lawful for man to utter. It is to God: not to you, who cannot take it in. For whether we are sober. By condescension. For you. Because we so speak that you can take it in. These are the angels of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: You shall see heaven opened, and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man; these same angels Jacob saw on the ladder ascending and descending.
5.14: 5.14 For the charity of Christ, etc. Because Christ died for us out of charity, it is established that all had died in Adam; for whom Christ died, to free them from death. Lest this grace be useless to men, the apostles, to draw them on, necessarily praise themselves; for through the glory and merit of the apostles the grace and benefit of Christ is recognized. If one for all. That is, if Christ for all as far as he is concerned, though he did not benefit all, therefore all men also ought to die for his honor.
5.15: 5.15 That they who live in the body should not live for themselves, but for the will of God. Which indeed they ought: because although Christ was weak and injured even to death, yet now after the resurrection he is not so, but appears what he seemed to be. Hence: When you shall have lifted up the Son of man, then you shall know that I am he, John 8. Let them therefore repay him as God, not only as man who suffered for them.
5.16: 5.16 We know no one. That is, we praise. After the flesh. That is, seeking his own, not the things of Christ: temporal, not eternal. Nor ought anyone to do this, because although Christ was mortal as I am, by which I thought him to be only man, while I was an unbeliever: yet now he is immortal, and so we are secure about the reward. If anyone therefore is in Christ born again new, for him mortality has already passed in hope, and will pass, and a new immortality will be given. Or, if anyone is new, the old law has passed from him, and he has a new. No one not after the flesh. He holds the future life with so certain a hope as though it were already present: which was fulfilled in Christ rising, which is not after the flesh: not that we shall not rise in the same substance of flesh, but not in the same quality of corruption, which is signified by the name of flesh. And if we have known after the flesh. Because although as an unbeliever he understood that Christ was promised in the law after the flesh, so as to observe legal things and command them to be observed: yet now after conversion he no longer believes it to be so, but the shadow wholly ceases.
5.17: 5.17 The old things. Altogether the Old Testament and all things pertaining to the old man, that thus. The new things. The New Testament has come, and all things of the new man. The old things. Such as the error of idolatry, to which the knowledge of the one true God has succeeded.
5.19: 5.19 God was. By this the Father is understood to be in the Son, and the Son in the Father, because their substance is one. There is unity where there is no diversity: and therefore each is in the other, because their image and likeness is one.
5.20: 5.20 Be reconciled. We are reconciled by confessing sins, and doing penance to him who reconciles us to himself.
5.21: 5.21 He made him sin for us. It is the usage of the Old Testament that sacrifices for sins are called sins, or sin is called the likeness of sinful flesh. Hence it is said: Of sin he destroyed or condemned sin, that is of the likeness of sinful flesh: because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. So also curse is taken for death, which came from the curse of God, that what is said in the law may be understood as truly said: Cursed is everyone that hangs on a tree, Deuteronomy 21. What is it that he says, cursed? that is, you are earth, and to earth you shall return, Genesis 3. What is it that he says, every one? because Christ, who hung on the tree, since he was the true life, died a true death, not feigned.
6.1: 6.1 That not in vain. The grace of God is remission of sins, which he receives in vain who will not exercise himself in good works, or who trusts in legal things.
6.2: 6.2 Now is the time. Which is not in the old law, or now, not tomorrow, not after a year: because immediately at the death of the faithful salvation is given.
6.3: 6.3 That our ministry be not blamed. Which would certainly happen if what we taught by word we did not show by the example of work.
6.4: 6.4 As the ministers of God. These do not flatter, like the false ones seeking gain. In much patience, in tribulations. In so many hardships, the burden of Christ is light and rest, within the Holy Spirit giving life, and hope of the future softening all things, for love makes all things cruel and immense easy and almost nothing. And according to this understand what is said: Come to me, all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you, Matthew 11. And again: Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet, ibid., etc.
6.6: 6.6 In chastity, in knowledge, that all may know how to act chastely, mixing in nothing of adulterous opinion. In sweetness, in the Holy Spirit: that is, sweet and affable according to God, not like those who by sweet speeches seduce the hearts of the innocent. In charity unfeigned. Feigned is that which deserts in adversity.
6.7: 6.7 In the power of God. Let us not hope in man or in goods; if there is anything good, let us attribute it to God. Or he says this because he who has the aforesaid works miracles for the conversion of unbelievers.
6.8: 6.8 By honor and dishonor. Let us show ourselves as ministers of God. By honor. If we are glorious among men, or ignoble and despised, let us not be puffed up by it, nor sink or grieve. In the same way if we are defamed for some crime let us have good fame for some work. Likewise let us show ourselves held by some as deceivers, which is false. And he does not say simply, held deceivers, but adds: as, and thence is the infamy. And among others held as truthful. As if he said: this is true, yet let us neither be proud of good esteem nor grieve at evil. Likewise held among others as chastised, etc.
6.10: 6.10 As sorrowful. Enemies thought the apostles would not escape the threats of the wicked. They by the help of God are safe from present and future death. Possessing all things. Such are those who, casting away earthly riches, already hold the heavenly through faith. As having nothing, they possess all things, who, retaining earthly things for use or the work of mercy, hope sometime to have the heavenly riches. It was the glory of the apostles to possess nothing at all, to be without solicitude: and to possess both things and their owners, because all things were laid at their feet.
6.11: 6.11 Our mouth. As if he said: I have said many things about you, but all these things, said amply and diffusely, look to correcting you, O Corinthians, and not to my pride; so you are foolish who dismissed me.
6.14: 6.14 Bear not the yoke, etc. The reason is, because you are just, they unjust: and therefore in nothing ought you to communicate with them.
6.15: 6.15 And what agreement has Christ. As Christ and Belial do not agree, so neither Christian and any unbeliever. Likewise the temple of God has nothing to do with idols; and because you are the temple of God, therefore you ought not to communicate with those who are the temple of the devil.
6.16: 6.16 With idols? He forbids idols to be worshiped, because they separate from the one God. In all these ways he shows that fellowship with the false is to be avoided. For I will dwell. This can be understood of the bodily conversation which Christ passed among men. And Christ says: I will dwell among them and walk, Baruch 3, that is, I will bodily converse among them. Hence elsewhere: He was seen on earth, and conversed with men; and the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, John 1. And this Christ is our God, and the Church is his people: and therefore the Apostle wishes them separated from all contamination.
7.1: 7.1 From all iniquity. Namely of the mind: which is then done if we follow the fear of God, because he who does these things without God is holy of the world, not of God. From all defilement of the flesh. That is of carnal observance, and perfecting sanctification which belongs only to the Holy Spirit.
7.3: 7.3 To die together. Either that you may suffer with me, or that you may be crowned with me.
7.4: 7.4 I am filled with consolation. Through those already corrected, he invites others to correction. I overabound, etc. This happens to the Apostle when he sees those advancing for whom he suffers.
7.5: 7.5 Our flesh. He says flesh, because in adversities the soul which is in the body that suffers rests in hope of the future. Without. This is understood of open enemies, within of false brethren, who are more hardly borne. Or from those who are without there is tribulation: from these, namely the faithful who are within, that is in the Church, fears lest they be moved. Or of those who are within, that is in the Church, in body, not in mind: in name, not in man, that is of false brethren, as before.
7.7: 7.7 With which he was comforted in you. Because I saw Titus comforted in you, and I have been comforted.
7.8: 7.8 And if I did regret. He says this lest he seem inhuman, who would rejoice at the sadness of others. Seeing. As if he said, I do not regret, but rejoice. Seeing that, that is although I see that the Epistle made you sad; hence at first I grieved, and I regretted.
7.9: 7.9 You were made sorrowful. Not with anger, which makes men worse, but with shame, which corrects.
7.10: 7.10 Penance unto salvation. The satisfaction of penance is to cut off the causes of sins, and not to give entrance to their suggestions. But of the world, etc. While the sinner grieves that he has been detected.
7.11: 7.11 For behold. Sorrow according to God works repentance unto salvation: because the things that lead to salvation work solicitude. What carefulness in you. He who repents is careful not to sin again, and does not excuse himself but confesses: which is to defend himself from hell: and he desires to be reformed, who knows himself deformed by sin, and has zeal for good works, and avenges in himself what he has committed. You have shown, etc. That is, you have shown by punishing him who committed the incest, that you are uncontaminated by the business, that is the grave sin of him who had his father's wife, in consenting to which you had been defiled.
7.12: 7.12 He that did the wrong. Such as he who committed incest. Or he touches those whom above in the first Epistle he said had done wrongs and frauds to brethren. And he shows that he wrote no more for the sake of those who sinned, that they be forgiven, than for the sake of the Church, which sympathizes and is indignant with everyone suffering insult or fraud. And this is what he says: Therefore though I wrote to you, not so much for him that did the wrong, that is fraud to his neighbor, nor for him that suffered the fraud, but to make manifest our solicitude, which, etc. He shows he has solicitude for the whole people, that is that the unjust be amended and the polluted sanctified, and reconciled to the Church.
7.13: 7.13 More abundantly. As if he said of both, that is of your correction and of the joy of Titus. But more abundantly we rejoiced at the joy of Titus, because the Apostle rejoiced not only over those corrected, but also over others whom he hoped to be corrected.
7.14: 7.14 But as, etc. In correcting, the truth of the one rebuking appears, when those rebuked amend themselves. For when the corrected are amended, they bear witness to the one who rebuked. Showing therefore his preaching true through their efficacy, the Apostle says: But as all things in truth, etc. And his bowels, etc. Holy affection is in all good.
8.1: 8.1 Now we make known to you. Here (where he treats of those corrected) mention is made of collections: because he does not seek from others, whom he cannot persuade. Or, as other codices have, to whom it does not profit to give their own.
8.2: 8.2 That in much experience. The abundant grace of theirs was in much experience of tribulation. Because they were not scandalized at the tribulation of Paul and Silas done there, but with joy received the word, proved by their sufferings. And the deepest. Slender in substance, rich in giving: because they wrought with a pure conscience.
8.5: 8.5 First amending themselves to the Lord, then offering their own things to the brethren. It was not otherwise to be accepted, because gifts blind the eyes and bend the rights of authority. But those who give lest they be rebuked do not have the fruit of giving.
8.8: 8.8 Not commanding, etc. I have not only asked Titus, but I myself say that you should abound, not as commanding. That is, not as imposing a penance, because thus the Corinthians would be held as if by a vow.
8.9: 8.9 He became poor. He does not say, he became poor, when he had been rich: but, when he was rich. For he took on poverty, and did not lose riches: within rich, without poor; God hidden in riches, man appearing in poverty. That by his poverty. For through his poverty we cast away the rags of iniquity, that we may be clothed with the robe of immortality. All therefore have become rich, believing in the poor Christ. Let no one therefore despise himself, poor in his cell, rich in conscience. He sleeps more securely on the ground than a rich man in purple on gold. Do not therefore be afraid to approach with your beggary him who, clothed in our poverty, where he made himself poor, enriched us.
8.10: 8.10 But also to will. As if he said: Some of yours had willed, others had begun: now let both perfect it.
8.13: 8.13 But by equality. Let each divide with the saints as much as he has, because no more is required than what he ought to keep for himself: thus Zacchaeus gave half of his goods to the poor.
8.14: 8.14 That there may be equality. Not that they do not differ in splendor: but because the same is for all, and there will be sufficiency for all. As it is written. Of the manna, in sign of this thing.
8.15: 8.15 He that gathered much had not more. The saints have more in the hope of the future, those less who are rich in time, and yet there they will be made equal. That as here they sustain the want of the saints, so there they may be sustained by them, and become rich in the eternal good. He that gathered much had not more. So he who gives much, being rich, and he who gives little, being poor, if the will of both is equal, have an equal reward.
8.18: 8.18 And we have sent. The Apostle sent two brethren with Titus, but does not name them, perhaps because the Corinthians did not know them, nor had they yet had experience of them. But since the multitude of the money collected is enough to give the wicked occasion for suspicion, he provides security; therefore, he says, we have sent such, and not one only, but two and three. He commends them not from the Gospel, nor from election alone, but also because they have been approved, and for that reason chosen, so that nothing may be suspected.
8.19: 8.19 In this grace. That is, the preaching to the Gentiles to which I am appointed, and I wish it.
8.20: 8.20 Avoiding this. The Apostle does not wish to seem too negligent in the care of the saints, and therefore forewarns that his solicitude may appear as forethought. In this part. Of doctrine and miracles, so that it be said, He preaches well, but is not mindful of the saints, as the other apostles are, and as was commanded him.
8.21: 8.21 Before God. For our sake our conscience is enough for us: for your sake our good name ought not to be defiled but to flourish in you. There are two things, conscience and fame: conscience for yourself, fame for your neighbor: he who, trusting his conscience, neglects his fame, is cruel.
8.22: 8.22 Confidence. As if he said: Did he go out of confidence in you? and for Titus and Luke with whom he gladly went.
8.23: 8.23 Whether. Or whether through your fathers the apostles of the Churches for the glory of God, that is, because they themselves are apostles of the Churches, this is of the glory of God, of Christ, that is to the glory of Christ: because in them is the glory not of men but of Christ.
8.24: 8.24 The proof. That is your charity which you have shown to others, and our boasting which you have likewise shown to be true, now show, by receiving these well, and this in the face of the Churches, that others may take example from you.
9.2: 9.2 And your emulation. By the emulation of the Corinthians other Churches (when they heard that they had first been entangled in errors and afterwards had become of good will) were stirred to good work.
9.4: 9.4 Lest we be ashamed. For if what the Apostle testified of them is not found true, he will blush and they themselves will be the more confounded.
9.6: 9.6 He who sows sparingly. He does not sow sparingly who, having little, gives little, if his mind is ready to give more if he had more.
9.7: 9.7 Not out of sadness. He who gives unwillingly through present shame has no reward. For the cheerful giver, he who gives to be rid of the tedium of the one asking, not to refresh the bowels of the needy, loses both merit and the thing. He gives largely who has the affection of giving, even if he has nothing to give.
9.8: 9.8 To abound, etc. For though what the one having little gives is small, yet it abounds, because it is done with right judgment: because the question is not how much, but in what spirit it is given.
9.9: 9.9 For righteousness. He is just who regards the goods of the world as common, for the end of an eternal reward.
9.10: 9.10 The increase of the fruits. Righteousness is holiness and good life: and thence fruits, that is, eternal recompense. The increase of almsgiving: for which both here the virtues and in the future the glory will be increased.
9.11: 9.11 Which works. That is, the liberality itself is the cause why thanks are given to God, of whose liberality we are the ministers.
9.15: 9.15 Thanks to God. For the mutual need and the mutual supply of the need of the provincials of Christ and the soldiers of Christ he gives thanks to God. Here he dealt with carnal things toward them, and after he dealt with spiritual things toward these, as though full of joys he cries out: I give thanks, etc.
10.1: 10.1 Now I Paul myself. He begins to deal with the uncorrected who followed the false apostles and thought the Apostle fierce, as if he said: I invite the corrected to almsgiving: Paul truly humble, not proud, I who admonish others to alms, the same to you as to them, I beseech, I say, etc.
10.3: 10.3 We do not war according to the flesh. For we do not exercise the warfare given us by God according to the flesh, that is, for earthly advantage.
10.4: 10.4 For the destruction of fortifications. That counsels fortified by the diverse craftiness of men or demons may be destroyed. Fortifications, etc. The fortifications are the hearts of unbelievers, which the devil holds and fortifies with diverse errors, lest the word of God enter through faith, or by the likeness of fortifications. And to overcome these let the arms of the Apostle's warfare avail, and he shows the parts of that fortification, namely, counsels.
10.6: 10.6 And having in readiness. Because nothing reproaches us so as to make us less bold. To revenge, etc. Then one avenges disobedience when he condemns it through obedience. Then he destroys it when he leads those who resist to the faith. And this is a worthy revenge, that perfidy be condemned by those by whom it was defended.
10.7: 10.7 Things that are according to the appearance. I have said many things by which I showed you that you ought to follow us rather than the false apostles, as if he said: If what I have said is not enough for you, why should you follow me rather than the false apostles? See these things which are according to the appearance, that is, they are so evident as those which lie before the eyes.
10.8: 10.8 I shall not be ashamed. Because it is both true, and not for my glory, but this is said for your profit.
10.9: 10.9 But that I may not be thought. Here he says that when present he will fulfill in deed what he threatens in word when absent. He says this on the occasion of that sentence: ready to avenge all disobedience: that, he says, I may not be thought by you to terrify only by words, and not fulfill in deed (which is less than words), know that I will fulfill by deeds less than by words.
10.11: 10.11 Let such a one think this, etc. JEROME. Let no one think that I threaten those things, etc., down to and I show myself strong to sinners through severity. Such. Because if we stroked your vices, then we should not build up but destroy.
10.12: 10.12 For we dare not, etc. Such we shall be in deed, because we are not like the false apostles, who usurp power to themselves and stroke vices. And this is: We do not insert ourselves among some, that is the false apostles who commend, that is usurp power. Which is, we do not place ourselves in their number, that we should usurp power, but we have received it from God. Nor do we compare ourselves with them so as, like them, to flatter you and stroke your vices: which even one having power could do.
10.13: 10.13 But we, etc. As those who by usurping glory beyond measure. But according to the measure. For by the nod of God he was admonished to evangelize the Corinthians. It had been apportioned to each to whom they should be directed in preaching, that each might have some peoples of his own, of whose faith to glory. But to the rule of the Apostle belonged all those whom he had founded in the faith: who had been sent by God to all.
10.15: 10.15 Not in other men's labors. To do this would be to glory beyond measure; but having hope in you: that is, to be magnified through you among others, and to evangelize according to our rule, that is, according to what was enjoined by God, not having hope to glory in another's rule.
10.17: 10.17 But he that glories. I will not glory in another's rule. Likewise he that glories, that is wishes to exercise power, let him glory in the Lord, that is, in the measure given by God.
10.18: 10.18 But whom God. God commends him, and he is approved, whom he holds worthy, and sends to preach his gift: whom he does not send, he does not commend, because he preaches unsent.
11.1: 11.1 Would that you could bear, etc. As if: I glory in the government (which seems folly). But would that you could bear, etc. He calls folly the boasting according to the flesh, lest in it he seem inferior to them, though he himself does not care, but it profits the Corinthians that he speak of it. Of my folly. Because it is said: Let your lips not praise you, but your neighbor's. Bear with me. As if he said: Even if I am burdensome, bear it patiently.
11.2: 11.2 I am jealous. Jealousy is a movement of mind on account of another's state, either toward good or toward evil. Here it is of love, not of envy, because he loves them with the jealousy of God, that is which God inspires by his spirit, and by this he shows that what he will say he will say out of love for them, not that they may profit to his praise but to their own progress. You to one. He descends from the plural to the singular, wishing the whole Church to be understood a virgin, and to preserve in all its true members virginity of mind (even if not of body). Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body: this virginity is of few. Virginity of heart is uncorrupted faith: this is of all the faithful.
11.3: 11.3 But I fear. JEROME. The serpent seduced Eve by lying about God, etc., down to or he affirms eternal life not to be, against the authority of all the Scriptures.
11.4: 11.4 For if he who comes. Not sent. You would rightly bear. If something greater were for you through them than through us, then you would rightly bear. He pronounces anathema on the Galatians if they received another, which would certainly not be greater, but contrary.
11.5: 11.5 For I suppose. Above he dealt with the false apostles, now with the true, to whom Paul seemed inferior; because he had not lived with Jesus.
11.6: 11.6 For though I be rude. This does not pertain to the apostles, because they were not eloquent, but to the false ones, who composed words. The unskilled in speech therefore is not guilty before God, but he who has not the knowledge of God, which pertains to salvation.
11.7: 11.7 Because freely the Gospel. I did not do less, but more: because freely, whence you are angry with me, and put others before me: though this is not a sin, but a glory.
11.10: 11.10 There is truth. JEROME. As Christ once decreed, and did not deny, it is necessary that I also, not having lied, do thus. That wherein they glory. They glory in receiving, but I not receiving, they will not receive. For such, etc. Let them be found even as we. That is, like us. In which, that is in this, that they glory to be like us.
11.13: 11.13 Transforming themselves. To tempt those whom it is thus needful to instruct. Or to deceive as is just. For this the great mercy of God is necessary, lest anyone, when he thinks he has good angels as friends, have bad demons, feigned friends; and suffer them as enemies the more harmful, the more cunning and deceitful.
11.15: 11.15 Whose end. That is, the recompense given at the end of life will be according to their works, because as the false ones sought perishable things, so they themselves shall perish, and as ministers of eternal righteousness, so they themselves will be eternal.
11.17: 11.17 What I speak. In this substance of glory, that is, in the glory of the flesh, which they think substance, that is, they so love it as though they believed they subsist by it. But as it were in folly. Because these things seem to pertain to the swelling of the flesh, where folly is. For it is folly for someone to praise himself. But because the Apostle does it not for himself but for God, therefore he says, as it were in folly.
11.20: 11.20 He strikes. That is, deceives. He is struck in the face upon whose mouth injury is inflicted. Certain Jews did this who, because they were of the race of Abraham, disparaged them for being uncircumcised and set themselves above them, claiming for themselves the nobility of the flesh: whom the Corinthians tolerated and preferred to the Apostle.
11.22: 11.22 Hebrews. Hebrews are so called from Eber, who alone at the confusion of tongues kept the natural language. And because there are many Hebrews who are not Israelites, as proselytes, he adds: They are Israelites, so am I.
11.23: 11.23 As less wise. AMBROSE. He shows that he was forced to break out into his own praise. In labors. The occasion found, he touches even the true apostles, than whom he labored more, lest grace seem less in him.
11.24: 11.24 Five times by the Jews. It was the custom of the Jews in the synagogue to scourge those acting against the law, for the sake of correction. Hence they scourged Paul, who impugned the law, five times, and in each correction gave him thirty-nine strokes, remitting the fortieth out of mercy. One less. At the last time the thong was withdrawn. Or, in each beating, one less.
11.26: 11.26 In perils of robbers, etc. Whom the devil (since he could not kill him in the city) stirred up against him on the road, although he carried nothing that robbers would desire.
11.27: 11.27 In hunger. Where then is the promise of God: Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you? Luke 12. But the physician to whom we have once committed ourselves knows when to apply, when to withdraw these aids.
11.28: 11.28 Solicitude. The greater the charity, the greater the wounds from the sins of others. Hence: He that adds knowledge, adds also sorrow.
11.29: 11.29 Am I not on fire? All tribulations burn, but not to consumption, rather to purification. This affection purifies: because it comes from charity. All who suffer scandal are the frying pan of those who have charity, that is of the bones which bear the flesh, that is of the perfect who carry and rule the carnal; hence: And my bones are fried in a frying pan.
11.31: 11.31 I lie not. Because he bears me witness by signs and wonders.
12.2: 12.2 I know a man. As of another, both the matter is told and boasting is avoided. Whether in the body, or, etc. The Apostle did not know this, whether when he was rapt the soul was in the body or had wholly gone out of the body, so that the body lay dead, or whether, according to some other manner of a living body where the soul was, his mind was taken to see or hear the ineffable things of that vision. And because this was uncertain, perhaps for that reason he said, whether in the body or out of it. Rapt. Raised contrary to nature. Even to the third heaven. That is, to the knowledge of the Deity. The first heaven is the airy; the second, the firmament; the third spiritual, where angels and holy souls of God enjoy contemplation.
12.4: 12.4 He was caught up. THEOPHYLACT. See his very great lowliness and humility, how as of another he recounts these things: for of this, he says, I will glory. But for whose sake (if another was rapt) do you glory? So he says these things of himself. Secret words. An intimation of the secret essence of God, as it were through words.
12.6: 12.6 Above that which, etc. For if I related great and more things, perhaps some would think me not to be weak, but an immortal man, or an angel, etc.; and therefore I speak sparingly of myself.
12.7: 12.7 And lest the greatness. I refrain from glorying much, lest another think. And therefore a thorn was given, pricking the flesh. Who? a malignant angel sent by Satan, to buffet, that is to repress every motion of pride by inflicting tribulations, or by tempting (as some say) through lust. But a temptation which is not consented to is not sin, but matter for exercising virtue.
12.9: 12.9 He said to me. By inspiration, or by an angel. For power is made perfect in infirmity. It is the perfection of virtues that has weakness opposed to it, with which it may rightly contend: and therefore I will glory in infirmities, not unwillingly but gladly.
12.11: 12.11 I am become foolish. In all these commendations I seem foolish, but it is your fault, who ought to have commended me against the false apostles.
12.12: 12.12 In all patience. He mentions patience first, which pertains to morals: because he bore them long, like impatient sick persons, so that by applying the power of signs he might cure their wounds as by medicine. And in mighty deeds. Mighty deed is a kind of signs and wonders, that is every miracle. A sign, which at any time signifies something, and is a kind of wonder. A wonder, which in the future. Or sign and wonder in things that are against nature, mighty deed in things that are not against nature, such as to free from disease by the laying on of hands and prayer.
12.14: 12.14 For neither ought, etc. Carnal fathers gather for their children, but it is fitting that spiritual fathers receive support from their children. Here he proves himself so unwilling to receive that he transfers the case of the carnal father to the spiritual one: and says he not only spends for their salvation, but is ready even to die.
12.15: 12.15 And will be spent, etc. Perfect charity is this, that one be ready even to die for the brethren. But does it come so as soon as it is born? When it is born, it is nourished: when nourished, it is strengthened: when strengthened, it is perfected: when it has come to perfection, it says: I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.
12.19: 12.19 Of old you think. As if he said: For some time perhaps you think that I say as a defendant by way of excuse that I did not burden you, but I say (God who knows being witness) that I did not circumvent you, and not proudly, but in Christ, to magnify you.
12.21: 12.21 Lest again when I come, etc. CHRYSOSTOM. It is glory to punish, to reproach, to exact penalties, etc., down to but on account of his command. And have not done. It is not enough to change morals for the better and to depart from evils, unless for the things done satisfaction is made to the Lord by the sorrow of penance, by the groan of humility, by the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with almsgiving cooperating.
13.2: 13.2 I will not spare. After so many corrections, if any do not amend, they ought not to be spared.
13.3: 13.3 Or do you seek a proof. It is the custom of divine Scripture to attribute to the person of God what he does in us, as the Apostle attributes the very speaking to him by whose gift he spoke, that is Christ. Who is not weak in you, but has appeared powerful when he gave gifts. Having experienced this, let them not doubt that they can be punished by him.
13.4: 13.4 For we also are weak. Christ lives who had before been weak. For we also, far lesser, though weak in him, that is though in imitation of him we suffer many things from the faithless, yet we shall live, that is we shall have power through him in judging you. Or, we shall live with him, that is in like blessedness with him: and this from the power of God; which is such in you, that is in your consciences: In you. Toward you. Death inflicted by the faithless is life toward believers, because rising by the power of God they will live with Christ.
13.7: 13.7 Now we pray, etc. The Apostle prays this, that when they do well he may find nothing in them to be rebuked, and so they appear reprobate: for they seem approved while they judge sinners. So then if there are none whom he may judge, authority ceasing, they seem as if reprobate. Let us be reprobate, that is let us appear reprobate, having nothing to avenge or judge.
13.9: 13.9 For we rejoice, etc. JEROME. We rejoice if it is not necessary that our power appear, as Peter's appeared in Sapphira and Ananias.
13.10: 13.10 According to the power. Again he shows that he does not desire to abuse power over them, adding that he received it not for destruction but for edification, whence he adds: Not unto destruction. Those who are corrected are not destroyed, but, corrected, are built up.
13.11: 13.11 Rejoice, brethren. That is, work well that you may be able to have true joy. And the God of peace shall be with you. From this you will have peace from his love, from this the removal of all evils. This peace has saved the world, ended a long war, joined earth to heaven, this made men angels. Let me imitate it. For love is the mother of innumerable goods, through it we have been saved, through it we obtain all ineffable goods.
13.13: 13.13 The grace. He wishes the whole Trinity to bless them. He assigns to each what is fitting. Grace, that is remission, to the Son; charity to the Father, who out of love sent the Son; communion to the Spirit, through whom union is made. And the charity of God. The love of God sent Christ, whose grace saves. And that we may possess this grace of salvation, the communion of the Holy Spirit made, or let the Spirit himself be so with you that he may communicate and confer on you both the grace of Christ and the charity of God. As if: May the whole Trinity be with you, giving grace for what has been committed and charity through the Spirit.
